table.data_collection_started: Yes, we already collected the data.
table.research_questions:
The goal of the present study is to replicate and extend previous findings on socio-affective dynamics related to psychopathy (Vize et al., 2025). 

Aim 1: Examine whether psychopathic traits moderate momentary associations between interpersonal stress/unpleasant interpersonal events and different forms of negative affect (anger, anxiety, remorse), with increased power to detect these effects relative to previous work. 

Aim 2: Examine whether psychopathic traits moderate the daily expression of specific maladaptive traits on days when there are also a greater number of interpersonally stressful/unpleasant interpersonal events.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Baseline Measures 

Comprehensive Assessment of Traits Relevant to Personality Disorder Static Form (CAT-PD-SF, v1.1; Simms, 2013). The CAT-PD-SF contains a large pool of items comprising 33 maladaptive personality traits. Each item is rated on a 0-4 Likert scale (0 = very untrue of me, 1 = moderately untrue of me, 2 = neither true or untrue of me, 3 = moderately true of me, 4 = very true of me). 

Following previous work that has used the CAT-PD-SF scale to study psychopathy (e.g., Kavish et al., 2019), but also work that has used the AMPD traits to assess psychopathy (e.g., Wygant et al., 2020), we will use the six facet scales of Manipulativeness, Callousness, Anger, Irresponsibility, Non-planfulness, and Risk-taking to assess antagonistic and disinhibitory components. Anxiousness (reverse-coded), Social Withdrawal (reverse-coded), and Exhibitionism will be used to assess the psychopathy specifier. We will also compute the mean of all three dimensions, representing a total psychopathy score.  

Ecological Momentary Assessment 

Abbreviated Positive and Negative Affect Schedule. Participants reported the degree to which they were experiencing negative and positive affect during each random survey. Negative affect was assessed using items adapted from the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS; Watson et al., 1988). Participants were asked “How [affective adjective] do you feel right now?” and used a 101-point sliding scale ranging from “0” (not at all) to “100” (extremely). Negative affect items that will be used for analyses are angry, frustrated, ashamed, guilty, and nervous. Positive affect items are confident, content, and excited.

Following Vize et al. (2025), we will examine three specific forms of negative affect: shame and guilt as a two-item composite, anger and frustration as a two-item composite, and nervous as a single item. The three positive affect items will be used to create a three-item composite of positive affect. 

Stressful/Unpleasant and Pleasant Interpersonal Events. After participants answered items assessing current positive and negative affect and impulsivity, they were asked if anything stressful had occurred since the last assessment. Participants were instructed to consider whether they themselves felt stressed when the event occurred, not whether they or another person would typically feel stressed in the same situation. If a stressful event occurred, participants answered additional questions about the event, including what type of event they encountered. The options were “argument/disagreement/conflict”, “social disappointment/let down”, “work/school related event”, “home related event”, “health issue or accident”, “event that happened to others”, and “other stressor.”  

Participants who indicated that they had not experienced a stressful event since the last assessment were asked if any of the following had occurred since the last assessment: “argument, disagreement, conflict”, “social disappointment/let down”, “difficulties involving work or school”, “difficulties at home”, “health issue or accident”, “negative event that happened to others”, or “other unpleasant event.” These selections were written to closely mirror the content of the stressful events but were presented in this manner to differentiate situation characteristics from the perception of stress. If participants indicated an unpleasant event occurred, they continued on to answer questions about the event. 

If participants did not indicate either a stressful or unpleasant event occurring since the last semester, participants were asked anything pleasant or positive had occurred since the previous assessment and could similarly select from a range of categories of pleasant events.

Our analyses will be focused on stressful/unpleasant events that participants classified as being an “argument/disagreement/conflict” or “social disappointment/let down” given their explicit interpersonal nature (13 different types in total). Similarly, we will focus on positive events that are interpersonal in nature (10 different types in total). The specific types of interpersonal stressors/unpleasant/pleasant events are listed below in Table 1.   

Inventory of Daily Expressions of Psychopathology (IDEP; https://osf.io/j9kyh). The IDEP was originally developed to assess personality disorder symptoms at the daily level (Wright & Simms, 2016). In the IDEP, items begin with the stem “Over the past 24 hours…” and are rated on a seven-point Likert scale from 0 (Not at All) to 7 (Very Much). 

An 81-item version of the IDEP was developed for use in the present study. Item stems remained the same, but ratings were made on a 101-point slider from 0 (Not at All) to 100 (Very Much). The 81-item version of the IDEP assesses 27 facets of psychopathology. Items related to positive symptoms of thought disorder were excluded because the sample did not include individuals diagnosed with thought disorders. 

For the present study, the following ten facets (each assessed with three items) will be used for analyses: Anger, Callousness, Domineering, Grandiosity/Entitlement, Hostile Aggression, Manipulativeness, Norm-violation, Irresponsibility, Impulsivity, and Risk Taking.

table.statistical_tests:
Basic descriptive analyses will examine the relations between antagonism, disinhibition, the psychopathy specifier, and the total score and ecological momentary outcomes. These will include average affect over the course of the EMA protocol (guilty/ashamed composite, angry/frustrated composite, positive affect composite, anxious), as well as the average number of different interpersonal events (stressful/unpleasant and positive). 

Analyses for Aim 1 will be carried out using multilevel SEM in Mplus. Each model will examine the momentary relation between interpersonal stress/unpleasant events and negative affect, using the three forms of negative affect described above as separate outcomes. Cross-level moderation effects will be tested for each dimension separately (antagonism, disinhibition, psychopathy specifier) and for the total score. Cross-level moderation will be tested by regressing the random slope from level 1 on the relevant level 2 predictor.  

A representative model focused on interpersonal stressful/unpleasant events and their relation with anger/frustration is included below, with antagonism as the level 2 predictor. Included covariates at level 1 for each model will be time of day, weekday/weekend (coded 0/1), and time since event. Covariates at level 2 will be sex (0=male, 1=female) and age. CAT-PD-SF composite scales will be grand-mean centered for analysis. 

********************************************************
Title: Antagonism and Momentary Relation between Int. Events and Anger/Frustration;

  Data: file is Psychop_momentary.csv;
  Variable:
  names are
      Ant		!Antagonism 
      Dis		!Disinhibition
      Ps_spec	!Psychopathy specifier
      Age
      Sex
      Wknd	!Weekday vs. Weekend
      Time	!Time of day
      T_since	!Time since the event
      Int_str	!Interpersonal stress/unpleasant event
      Ang		!Anger/frustration composite
      ID;		!Participant ID

  missing are all (-999); 
  cluster=id;

  usevariables =
  age sex
  time wknd t_since
  Ant Int_str Ang;

  within =  time wknd; 				!Variables at level-1 only
  between =  age sex Ant;			!Variables at level-2 only
  Define:
  center Ant (GRANDMEAN);
  center age (GRANDMEAN);

  Analysis:    
  type = twolevel random;	  
  estimator = bayes;				!Bayesian estimation with default priors 
  FBITERATIONS = 10000;			!10,000 MCMC iterations			

  Model:
  %WITHIN%
  rand_a | Ang on Int_str; 			!Within-person effect of Int. stress on anger
  Ang on time t_since wknd;

  %BETWEEN%
  rand_a on Ant; 				!Test of cross-level moderation
  Ang Int_str on Ant;				!Regress level-2 anger and int. stress on antagonism 
  rand_a Ang Int_str on age sex;			!Include age and sex as covariates at level-2
  Output:
  stdyx sampstat cinterval tech8;

********************************************************

Analyses for Aim 2 will be estimated in a similar fashion, but data will be aggregated to the daily level. We will also drop the within-person covariates of time of day and time since event. For stressful/unpleasant interpersonal events, they will be summed for each day, such that participants will have daily sum scores for the number of stressful/interpersonal events on a given day. The representative model below estimates the relation between daily number of stressful/unpleasant interpersonal events and IDEP-Anger.  

Title: Antagonism and Daily Relation between Int. Events and IDEP Anger;

  Data: file is Psychop_momentary.csv;
  Variable:
  names are
      Ant	!Antagonism 
      Dis		!Disinhibition
      Ps_spec	!Psychopathy specifier
      Age
      Sex
      Wknd	!Weekday vs. Weekend
      D_Int	!Daily count of interpersonal stress/unpleasant event
      Idep_ang	!IDEP-Anger
      ID;		!Participant ID

  missing are all (-999); 
  cluster=id;

  usevariables =
  age sex
  wknd 
  Ant D_Int IDEP_ang;

  within =  wknd; 				!Variables at level-1 only
  between =  age sex Ant;			!Variables at level-2 only
  Define:
  center Ant (GRANDMEAN);
  center age (GRANDMEAN);

  Analysis:    
  type = twolevel random;	  
  estimator = bayes;				!Bayesian estimation with default priors 	
  FBITERATIONS = 10000;			!10,000 MCMC iterations		

  Model:
  %WITHIN%
  rand_a | idep_ang on D_int; 		!Within-person effect daily int. stress on idep anger
  idep_ang on wknd;

  %BETWEEN%
  rand_a on Ant; 				!Test of cross-level moderation
  idep_ang D_int on Ant;			!Regress level-2 anger and int. stress on antagonism 
  rand_a idep_ang D_int on age sex;		!Include age and sex as covariates at level-2
  
  Output:
  stdyx sampstat cinterval tech8;

********************************************************

table.additional_comments:
Secondary Analysis 

For Aim 2 analyses, we will also test a different operationalization of daily interpersonal stress. For each stressful/unpleasant event, participants provided ratings (on a 0-100 sliding scale) of how stressful/unpleasant the event was when it occurred ("How stressful was this event when it happened?"; "How unpleasant was this event when it happened?"). Our secondary analyses will examine the aggregated daily ratings of stressfulness/unpleasantness in contrast to our primary analyses which will be focused on the number of interpersonal events at the daily level. 

Details on Points of Overlap with Previous Publications Using the AAPECS dataset 

We highlight important points of overlap between our proposed analyses and previous studies using the AAPECS dataset.

1.	Vize, C. E., Kaurin, A., & Wright, A. G. C. (2023). Personality Pathology and Momentary Stress Processes. Clinical Psychological Science. 

In Vize et al. (2023), broad CAT-PD domains were tested as moderators of specific within-person links between negative affect and momentary stress. The CAT-PD facet scales were combined to create domain scales of Negative Affectivity, Detachment, Psychoticism, Antagonism, and Disinhibition. 

Momentary stress was operationalized as any report of a stressful or unpleasant event occurring since the last EMA prompt. Preregistered MSEM testes were used to examine 1) within-person links among negative affect (items: angry, ashamed, guilty, nervous, sad, frustrated) and stress and 2) whether these links were enhanced by CAT-PD domain scales. table.research_questions:
The goal of the present study is to replicate and extend previous findings on socio-affective dynamics related to psychopathy (Vize et al., 2025). 

Aim 1: Examine whether psychopathic traits moderate momentary associations between interpersonal stress/unpleasant interpersonal events and different forms of negative affect (anger, anxiety, remorse), with increased power to detect these effects relative to previous work. 

Aim 2: Examine whether psychopathic traits moderate the daily expression of specific maladaptive traits on days when there are also a greater number of interpersonally stressful/unpleasant interpersonal events.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Baseline Measures 

Comprehensive Assessment of Traits Relevant to Personality Disorder Static Form (CAT-PD-SF, v1.1; Simms, 2013). The CAT-PD-SF contains a large pool of items comprising 33 maladaptive personality traits. Each item is rated on a 0-4 Likert scale (0 = very untrue of me, 1 = moderately untrue of me, 2 = neither true or untrue of me, 3 = moderately true of me, 4 = very true of me). 

Following previous work that has used the CAT-PD-SF scale to study psychopathy (e.g., Kavish et al., 2019), but also work that has used the AMPD traits to assess psychopathy (e.g., Wygant et al., 2020), we will use the six facet scales of Manipulativeness, Callousness, Anger, Irresponsibility, Non-planfulness, and Risk-taking to assess antagonistic and disinhibitory components. Anxiousness (reverse-coded), Social Withdrawal (reverse-coded), and Exhibitionism will be used to assess the psychopathy specifier. We will also compute the mean of all three dimensions, representing a total psychopathy score.  

Ecological Momentary Assessment 

Abbreviated Positive and Negative Affect Schedule. Participants reported the degree to which they were experiencing negative and positive affect during each random survey. Negative affect was assessed using items adapted from the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS; Watson et al., 1988). Participants were asked “How [affective adjective] do you feel right now?” and used a 101-point sliding scale ranging from “0” (not at all) to “100” (extremely). Negative affect items that will be used for analyses are angry, frustrated, ashamed, guilty, and nervous. Positive affect items are confident, content, and excited.

Following Vize et al. (2025), we will examine three specific forms of negative affect: shame and guilt as a two-item composite, anger and frustration as a two-item composite, and nervous as a single item. The three positive affect items will be used to create a three-item composite of positive affect. 

Stressful/Unpleasant and Pleasant Interpersonal Events. After participants answered items assessing current positive and negative affect and impulsivity, they were asked if anything stressful had occurred since the last assessment. Participants were instructed to consider whether they themselves felt stressed when the event occurred, not whether they or another person would typically feel stressed in the same situation. If a stressful event occurred, participants answered additional questions about the event, including what type of event they encountered. The options were “argument/disagreement/conflict”, “social disappointment/let down”, “work/school related event”, “home related event”, “health issue or accident”, “event that happened to others”, and “other stressor.”  

Participants who indicated that they had not experienced a stressful event since the last assessment were asked if any of the following had occurred since the last assessment: “argument, disagreement, conflict”, “social disappointment/let down”, “difficulties involving work or school”, “difficulties at home”, “health issue or accident”, “negative event that happened to others”, or “other unpleasant event.” These selections were written to closely mirror the content of the stressful events but were presented in this manner to differentiate situation characteristics from the perception of stress. If participants indicated an unpleasant event occurred, they continued on to answer questions about the event. 

If participants did not indicate either a stressful or unpleasant event occurring since the last semester, participants were asked anything pleasant or positive had occurred since the previous assessment and could similarly select from a range of categories of pleasant events.

Our analyses will be focused on stressful/unpleasant events that participants classified as being an “argument/disagreement/conflict” or “social disappointment/let down” given their explicit interpersonal nature (13 different types in total). Similarly, we will focus on positive events that are interpersonal in nature (10 different types in total). The specific types of interpersonal stressors/unpleasant/pleasant events are listed below in Table 1.   

Inventory of Daily Expressions of Psychopathology (IDEP; https://osf.io/j9kyh). The IDEP was originally developed to assess personality disorder symptoms at the daily level (Wright & Simms, 2016). In the IDEP, items begin with the stem “Over the past 24 hours…” and are rated on a seven-point Likert scale from 0 (Not at All) to 7 (Very Much). 

An 81-item version of the IDEP was developed for use in the present study. Item stems remained the same, but ratings were made on a 101-point slider from 0 (Not at All) to 100 (Very Much). The 81-item version of the IDEP assesses 27 facets of psychopathology. Items related to positive symptoms of thought disorder were excluded because the sample did not include individuals diagnosed with thought disorders. 

For the present study, the following ten facets (each assessed with three items) will be used for analyses: Anger, Callousness, Domineering, Grandiosity/Entitlement, Hostile Aggression, Manipulativeness, Norm-violation, Irresponsibility, Impulsivity, and Risk Taking.

table.statistical_tests:
Basic descriptive analyses will examine the relations between antagonism, disinhibition, the psychopathy specifier, and the total score and ecological momentary outcomes. These will include average affect over the course of the EMA protocol (guilty/ashamed composite, angry/frustrated composite, positive affect composite, anxious), as well as the average number of different interpersonal events (stressful/unpleasant and positive). 

Analyses for Aim 1 will be carried out using multilevel SEM in Mplus. Each model will examine the momentary relation between interpersonal stress/unpleasant events and negative affect, using the three forms of negative affect described above as separate outcomes. Cross-level moderation effects will be tested for each dimension separately (antagonism, disinhibition, psychopathy specifier) and for the total score. Cross-level moderation will be tested by regressing the random slope from level 1 on the relevant level 2 predictor.  

A representative model focused on interpersonal stressful/unpleasant events and their relation with anger/frustration is included below, with antagonism as the level 2 predictor. Included covariates at level 1 for each model will be time of day, weekday/weekend (coded 0/1), and time since event. Covariates at level 2 will be sex (0=male, 1=female) and age. CAT-PD-SF composite scales will be grand-mean centered for analysis. 

********************************************************
Title: Antagonism and Momentary Relation between Int. Events and Anger/Frustration;

  Data: file is Psychop_momentary.csv;
  Variable:
  names are
      Ant		!Antagonism 
      Dis		!Disinhibition
      Ps_spec	!Psychopathy specifier
      Age
      Sex
      Wknd	!Weekday vs. Weekend
      Time	!Time of day
      T_since	!Time since the event
      Int_str	!Interpersonal stress/unpleasant event
      Ang		!Anger/frustration composite
      ID;		!Participant ID

  missing are all (-999); 
  cluster=id;

  usevariables =
  age sex
  time wknd t_since
  Ant Int_str Ang;

  within =  time wknd; 				!Variables at level-1 only
  between =  age sex Ant;			!Variables at level-2 only
  Define:
  center Ant (GRANDMEAN);
  center age (GRANDMEAN);

  Analysis:    
  type = twolevel random;	  
  estimator = bayes;				!Bayesian estimation with default priors 
  FBITERATIONS = 10000;			!10,000 MCMC iterations			

  Model:
  %WITHIN%
  rand_a | Ang on Int_str; 			!Within-person effect of Int. stress on anger
  Ang on time t_since wknd;

  %BETWEEN%
  rand_a on Ant; 				!Test of cross-level moderation
  Ang Int_str on Ant;				!Regress level-2 anger and int. stress on antagonism 
  rand_a Ang Int_str on age sex;			!Include age and sex as covariates at level-2
  Output:
  stdyx sampstat cinterval tech8;

********************************************************

Analyses for Aim 2 will be estimated in a similar fashion, but data will be aggregated to the daily level. We will also drop the within-person covariates of time of day and time since event. For stressful/unpleasant interpersonal events, they will be summed for each day, such that participants will have daily sum scores for the number of stressful/interpersonal events on a given day.   Data: file is Psychop_momentary.csv;
  Variable:
  names are
      Ant	!Antagonism 
      Dis		!Disinhibition
      Ps_spec	!Psychopathy specifier
      Age
      Sex
      Wknd	!Weekday vs. Weekend
      D_Int	!Daily count of interpersonal stress/unpleasant event
      Idep_ang	!IDEP-Anger
      ID;		!Participant ID

  missing are all (-999); 
  cluster=id;

  usevariables =
  age sex
  wknd 
  Ant D_Int IDEP_ang;

  within =  wknd; 				!Variables at level-1 only
  between =  age sex Ant;			!Variables at level-2 only
  Define:
  center Ant (GRANDMEAN);
  center age (GRANDMEAN);

  Analysis:    
  type = twolevel random;	  
  estimator = bayes;				!Bayesian estimation with default priors 	
  FBITERATIONS = 10000;			!10,000 MCMC iterations		

  Model:
  %WITHIN%
  rand_a | idep_ang on D_int; 		!Within-person effect daily int. stress on idep anger
  idep_ang on wknd;

  %BETWEEN%
  rand_a on Ant; 				!Test of cross-level moderation
  idep_ang D_int on Ant;			!Regress level-2 anger and int. stress on antagonism 
  rand_a idep_ang D_int on age sex;		!Include age and sex as covariates at level-2
  
  Output:
  stdyx sampstat cinterval tech8;

live_data_statements: Participants 311 participants were recruited from the [redacted for peer review] metropolitan area through the [redacted for peer review]'s Clinical Translational Science Institute's participant registry and flyers posted in the metropolitan area.

These participants were pre-screened using three subscales from the Interpersonal Problems-Personality Disorder scale (IIP-PD; Pilkonis et al., 1996) to enrich the sample for a broad range of personality pathology.

Potential participants were administered these eighteen items during screening phone calls and were categorized as having low (sum scores less than or equal to ten), moderate (sum scores between eleven and sixteen), or high (sum scores greater than or equal to eighteen) levels of interpersonal difficulties.
Participants completed a baseline in-person lab session and an ambulatory assessment protocol.
Ninety-minute intervals were blocked randomly between receiving each survey prompt, and participants were allotted twenty minutes to initiate responding to the surveys before they expired.
Participants completed the Comprehensive Assessment of Traits Relevant to Personality Disorder-Static Form (CAT-PD-SF; Simms, 2013) during the baseline appointment.
Participants were asked "How [affective adjective] do you feel right now?"
Participants were instructed to consider whether they themselves felt stressed when the event occurred, not whether they or another person would typically feel stressed in the same situation.
Participants were also asked to rate how stressful the situation was, using a 0 (not at all) to 100 (extremely) sliding scale.

If participants did not indicate either a stressful or unpleasant event occurring since the last assessment, participants were asked anything pleasant or positive had occurred since the previous assessment and could similarly select from a range of categories of pleasant events.

info.title: An Examination of the DSM-5 Alternative Model of Psychopathy in Daily Life Psychopathic Traits and Reactions to Interpersonal Stress in Daily Life: An Examination of the DSM-5 Alternative Model of Psychopathy

text.text: The Alternative Model of Personality Disorders (AMPD) in DSM-5 represents psychopathy through the antisocial personality disorder domains of antagonism and disinhibition and a psychopathy specifier tied to boldness, but no research has examined how this model relates to functioning in daily life.

In a sample enriched for interpersonal difficulties (N = 296), we examined whether AMPD psychopathic traits moderated the effects of interpersonal events on momentary affect, and the effects of daily interpersonal stress on daily expressions of psychopathology, during a 14-to 21-day ecological momentary assessment protocol.

Multilevel structural equation models showed that stressful and unpleasant interpersonal events were robustly related to within-person increases in negative affect, particularly anger/frustration, and daily interpersonal stress was related to increased expression of most psychopathy-relevant traits (e.g., callousness, hostile aggression).
However, AMPD psychopathic traits rarely moderated these processes.

Exceptions included antagonism and disinhibition amplifying positive affect following positive interpersonal events, and the psychopathy specifier amplifying the association between daily stress and grandiosity/entitlement.
The AMPD components were primarily related to average levels of daily functioning.

Antagonism and disinhibition were related to higher negative affect and daily expressions of psychopathology, while the psychopathy specifier was related to higher positive affect and less daily expressions of psychopathology.

Replicating and extending prior work, these findings suggest that differences in average daily functioning associated with psychopathic traits are not explained by heightened or blunted reactivity to interpersonal stress, and raise questions about the role of the psychopathy specifier in the AMPD.

Psychopathy is a multifaceted personality disorder characterized by traits related to disinhibition (e.g., lack of planning, sensation seeking), antagonism (e.g., callousness, exploitativeness), and boldness (e.g., social dominance, emotional resilience) and is of significant interest due to its robust relation to harmful antisocial behaviors (De Brito et al., 2021).

text.text: This methodological gap in the research literature is important to address.
The problems associated with psychopathy, like those of other personality disorders, occur most often in the social situations that unfold within the ebb and flow of daily life (Hopwood, 2018).
text.formatted: The problems associated with psychopathy, like those of other personality disorders, occur most often in the social situations that unfold within the ebb and flow of daily life <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hopwood, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Psychopathic traits are therefore likely to be most consequential in specific interpersonal contexts, particularly stressful or conflictual ones, and EMA designs can capture these events as they occur.

Moreover, research has consistently demonstrated that maladaptive traits, including those related to psychopathy (e.g., antagonism), vary in their expression at the momentary and daily level (Wright & Simms, 2016; Zimmermann et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Moreover, research has consistently demonstrated that maladaptive traits, including those related to psychopathy (e.g., antagonism), vary in their expression at the momentary and daily level <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Wright & Simms, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Zimmermann et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: EMA designs thus allow psychopathic traits to be studied in two complementary ways: as stable dispositions that moderate how individuals respond to momentary events, and as dynamic states that fluctuate from day to day.

Regarding the AMPD model of psychopathy, EMA designs can strengthen our understanding of how each individual component (antagonism, disinhibition, and the psychopathy specifier) and their combination relate to momentary outcomes.

Earlier work using momentary assessments has supported the idea that features of antagonism are related to higher average negative affect in daily life, as well as more consistent interpersonal coldness across interpersonal contexts (Vize et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Earlier work using momentary assessments has supported the idea that features of antagonism are related to higher average negative affect in daily life, as well as more consistent interpersonal coldness across interpersonal contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Vize et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, across three EMA samples, trait disinhibition was consistently associated with higher negative affect in daily life, above and beyond trait antagonism (Mostajabi & Wright, 2025).
text.formatted: Similarly, across three EMA samples, trait disinhibition was consistently associated with higher negative affect in daily life, above and beyond trait antagonism <ref type="bibr">(Mostajabi & Wright, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Disinhibition was also associated with less warmth during social interactions, but this effect was largely accounted for by antagonism, and disinhibition showed no consistent associations with positive affect or dominance.

Yet key questions that EMA designs are uniquely positioned to address are when and how the psychopathic traits influence maladaptive and adaptive functioning (e.g., within a stressful An Examination of the DSM-5 Alternative Model of Psychopathy in Daily Life interpersonal situation vs. in other contexts).
To date, very few studies have addressed these questions.
A recent exception is Vize et al. (2026), who examined socioaffective dynamics associated with psychopathic traits (assessed with PPI-based self-report measures) in two adult samples.
text.formatted: A recent exception is <ref type="bibr">Vize et al. (2026)</ref>, who examined socioaffective dynamics associated with psychopathic traits (assessed with PPI-based self-report measures) in two adult samples.

text.text: They examined both person-level outcomes (e.g., average hostile, sad, and positive affect; average ratings of negative and positive interactions) and within-person processes (e.g., changes in affect following negative interactions), including whether psychopathic traits moderated these processes.
Evidence linking psychopathic traits to average outcomes was mixed.
Impulsive Antisociality was the only trait with a replicable association, relating to higher average hostile affect in both samples.
Other effects emerged in only one sample: Impulsive Antisociality related to higher sad affect and more negative interactions, whereas Fearless Dominance related to lower hostile and sad affect.
Notably, PPI total scores were unrelated to all average outcomes in both samples, likely because the opposing effects of Impulsive Antisociality and Fearless Dominance offset one another.
Further, despite robust within-person effects (e.g., notable increases in hostile affect following negative interactions), psychopathic traits rarely moderated these processes.
Although these initial results provided valuable data on the momentary relations of traits related to psychopathy, Vize and colleagues (2026) pointed to several important directions for future work.
text.formatted: Although these initial results provided valuable data on the momentary relations of traits related to psychopathy, <ref type="bibr">Vize and colleagues (2026)</ref> pointed to several important directions for future work.

text.text: First, the sample sizes (Ns of 142 and 159) provided adequate power only for moderate or large effects.
These analyses may therefore have missed the smaller effects expected when relating traits derived from self-report questionnaires to EMA-based outcomes.

Second, the negative interaction measures were broad in scope and varied across samples, and psychopathic traits may exert their strongest influence in more specific interpersonal contexts (e.g., An Examination of the DSM-5 Alternative Model of Psychopathy in Daily Life interpersonally stressful situations).

Third, the divergent effects of Fearless Dominance and Impulsive Antisociality complicate interpretation of total scores and highlight the value of examining the total scores alongside narrower, more homogeneous trait dimensions.
The present study sought to address these limitations while being the first study to examine the AMPD model of psychopathy in daily life.

Using a larger sample (N = 296) and AMPD-aligned measures of antagonism, disinhibition, and the psychopathy specifier, we focus specifically on interpersonally stressful and unpleasant experiences, contexts in which psychopathic traits are theorized to be particularly consequential.

First, aiming to replicate findings from Vize and colleagues (2026), we tested whether AMPD psychopathic traits enhance or dampen within-person links between interpersonal stressful or unpleasant experiences and momentary negative affect, as well as the within-person links between positive interpersonal interactions and positive affect.

text.text: Participants 311 participants were recruited from the [redacted for peer review] metropolitan area through the [redacted for peer review]'s Clinical Translational Science Institute's participant registry and flyers posted in the metropolitan area.

These participants were pre-screened using three subscales from the Interpersonal Problems-Personality Disorder scale (IIP-PD; Pilkonis et al., 1996) to enrich the sample for a broad range of personality pathology.

text.text: The IIP-PD assesses distress associated with interpersonal problems, asking participants to rate 28 items on a Likert scale ranging from 0 to 4 (0 = "not at all",1 = "a little bit",2 = "moderately",3 = "quite a bit",4 = "extremely distressing").

Previous research has found that the measure can reliably discriminate between individuals who have maladaptive personality traits and those who do not through the administration of eighteen items from three specific subscales: Interpersonal sensitivity, interpersonal ambivalence, and aggression (Morse & Pilkonis, 2007; Pilkonis et al., 1996).

text.text: Potential participants were administered these eighteen items during screening phone calls and were categorized as having low (sum scores less than or equal to ten), moderate (sum scores between eleven and sixteen), or high (sum scores greater than or equal to eighteen) levels of interpersonal difficulties.

In the selected sample, the reliability for total IIP-PD scores was high (a = .89, ω = .92), and the final representation of participants was approximately 1-1-1 for each interpersonal difficulty level.

The final sample for analysis consisted of 296 2 individuals after excluding fourteen participants who failed to complete greater than ten surveys over the course of the EMA An Examination of the DSM-5 Alternative Model of Psychopathy in Daily Life protocol, and a single participant who was missing data on age, an included covariate in our models.

These participants fell between the ages of 18 and 40 (M = 28.0, SD = 6.39) and were 52.53% female (n=156), with sixty percent of participants reporting an annual family income less than or equal to $59,000.

The sample predominantly identified as White (71.38%, n = 212), and 13.47% participants identified as Black or African American (n = 40), 6.4% identified as Asian (n = 19), 8.08% identified as multiracial or "other" (n = 24), and two participants declined to provide their ethnicity. 191 participants (64.31%) had a lifetime history of receiving mentalhealth treatment, with 118 of those individuals reporting at the baseline visit that they were currently receiving treatment.
Participants completed a baseline in-person lab session and an ambulatory assessment protocol.
Each participant was compensated $50 for completing the 3-to-5-hour baseline session, and compensation for the ambulatory assessment period was based on survey response rates.
If 90% or greater of random surveys were answered during the EMA protocol, participants earned an additional $110 (for the 14-day protocol) or $160 (for the 21-day protocol).
Participants who completed less than 90% of surveys received prorated compensation, where the surveys completed in later weeks were valued higher.
Ambulatory assessment began the day following participant baseline appointments.
The assessment periods were initially established as 21 days (n = 37) and were shortened to 14 days (n = 260) early in the study with the goal of avoiding overburdening participants.
The surveys were administered on a pseudorandom schedule using the MetricWire smartphone application (MetricWire, 2019).
Six surveys were administered via push notifications per day in an approximately 12-hour time block which aligned appropriately with participant reported sleep-and-wake times.
Ninety-minute intervals were blocked randomly between receiving each survey prompt, and participants were allotted twenty minutes to initiate responding to the surveys before they expired.

In sum, we collected 20,379 random survey responses, with participants completing a mean of 68.62 surveys (SD = 20.94) over the course of the study; this represents an approximately 76.8% compliance rate for random survey completion.
Participants completed the Comprehensive Assessment of Traits Relevant to Personality Disorder-Static Form (CAT-PD-SF; Simms, 2013) during the baseline appointment.
The CAT-PD-SF contains 216 items assessing 33 maladaptive personality traits.
Each item is rated on a Likert scale from 0 (very untrue of me) to 4 (very true of me).

The 33 trait subscales have been shown to reflect five overarching factors (negative affectivity, disinhibition, detachment, antagonism, and psychoticism) in structural analyses and map onto corresponding factors established in other models of maladaptive personality (Wright & Simms, 2014).

text.text: Participants were asked "How [affective adjective] do you feel right now?"
and used a 101-point sliding scale ranging from 0 (not at all) to 100 (extremely) to report the intensity of feelings of shame, nervousness, sadness, anger, guilt, and frustration.
Positive affect items were confident, content, and excited.
We examined three specific forms of negative affect: shame and guilt as a two-item composite, anger and frustration as a two-item composite, and nervous as a single item.
The three positive affect items were used to create a three-item composite of positive affect.
After participants answered items assessing current positive and negative affect and impulsivity, they were asked if anything stressful had occurred since the last assessment.
Participants were instructed to consider whether they themselves felt stressed when the event occurred, not whether they or another person would typically feel stressed in the same situation.
If a stressful event occurred, participants answered additional questions about the event, including what type of event they encountered.

The options were "argument/disagreement/conflict", "social disappointment/let down", "work/school related event", "home related event", "health issue or accident", "event that happened to others", and An Examination of the DSM-5 Alternative Model of Psychopathy in Daily Life "other stressor."
Participants were also asked to rate how stressful the situation was, using a 0 (not at all) to 100 (extremely) sliding scale.

Participants who indicated that they had not experienced a stressful event since the last assessment were asked if any of the following had occurred since the last assessment: "argument, disagreement, conflict", "social disappointment/let down", "difficulties involving work or school", "difficulties at home", "health issue or accident", "negative event that happened to others", or "other unpleasant event."
These selections were written to closely mirror the content of the stressful events but were presented in this manner to differentiate situation characteristics from the perception of stress.

If participants indicated an unpleasant event occurred, they continued to answer questions about the event, including how unpleasant the event was using a 0 (not at all) to 100 (extremely) sliding scale.

If participants did not indicate either a stressful or unpleasant event occurring since the last assessment, participants were asked anything pleasant or positive had occurred since the previous assessment and could similarly select from a range of categories of pleasant events.

Our analyses focused on stressful/unpleasant events that participants classified as being an "argument/disagreement/conflict" or "social disappointment/let down" given their explicit interpersonal nature (13 different types in total).
Similarly, we focused on positive events that were interpersonal in nature (10 different types in total).
The specific types of interpersonal events participants could choose from are listed in the supplement (Table S1).

Our primary analyses used multilevel structural equation models (MSEMs) to estimate the relations between baseline predictors (the CAT-PD-derived AMPD psychopathy domains of antagonism, disinhibition, and the psychopathy specifier, as well as a psychopathy total score) and our selected outcome measures.
Like typical multilevel modeling approaches, MSEM partitions the overall variability in individuals' intensive longitudinal data into between-and within-person components.
MSEM offers additional advantages, including latent decomposition of between-and within-person variance in repeated assessment data (Sadikaj et al., 2021).
text.formatted: MSEM offers additional advantages, including latent decomposition of between-and within-person variance in repeated assessment data <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Sadikaj et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Between-person variance reflects individual differences in average responses and captures traitlike content.
Within-person variance reflects deviations from an individual's own average level from one occasion to the next.
Thus, within-person associations reflect how occasion-level deviations relate to one another.

All within-person regression paths (e.g., the relation between stressful interpersonal events and momentary anger/frustration) were estimated as random slopes, which allow individuals to differ in the strength of their within-person associations.
Including random slopes allowed us test whether the strength of any within-person associations varied as a function of individual differences in psychopathic traits (i.e., a cross-level interaction).
We tested this by regressing each random slope on the relevant between-person predictor.
All MSEMs were estimated in Mplus Version 8.10 (Muthén & Muthén, 2025) using Bayesian estimation with default, diffuse priors for all model parameters.

text.text: Each model was first estimated using the default convergence criterion (potential scale reduction values below 1.10).
Once convergence was established, each model was re-estimated with the number of MCMC iterations fixed at 10,000.
MSEMs were estimated separately for each psychopathy predictor (antagonism, disinhibition, psychopathy specifier, and total score) and each outcome.

Specifically, disinhibition was positively related to a greater frequency of stressful or unpleasant events over the protocol (b=0.01; 95% CI= 0.00; 0.01; β =.11; p=.015), while the psychopathy specifier was negatively related to the frequency of these events (b=-0.01; 95% CI= -0.01; 0.00; β =-.10; p=.024).

text.text: Consistent with that work, stressful and unpleasant interpersonal situations were robustly linked to within-person increases in negative affect, particularly anger/frustration, and at the daily level, to increases in the expression of psychopathic traits (e.g., anger, callousness, hostile aggression).
However, with some exceptions, psychopathic traits assessed at baseline rarely moderated these within-person processes.
The three components of daily variables-antagonism and disinhibition were generally related to maladaptive functioning and the psychopathy specifier was generally related to adaptive functioning.
These divergent effects meant that AMPD psychopathy total scores obscured meaningful differences among components.
Together, these findings clarify how the components of AMPD psychopathy relate to everyday functioning and highlight important opportunities for future EMA work focused on psychopathic traits.

At the within-person level, there was consistent evidence that stressful and unpleasant interpersonal events led to subsequent increases in all forms of negative affect, while positive interpersonal events were linked to subsequent increases in positive affect.
In these momentary analyses, there was no evidence that AMPD psychopathic traits enhanced or dampened within-person reactivity to stressful or unpleasant interpersonal events.

This general scarcity of cross-level moderation effects for such events is consistent with Vize et al. (2026), despite using a larger sample, more homogenous scales to tap the antagonistic, disinhibitory, and boldness-related features of psychopathy, and assessments focused on specific stressful or unpleasant interpersonal events.

text.text: In the general personality processes work, researchers have historically distinguished personality differences in exposure to stressful events and reactivity to those events once they occur (e.g. Bolger & Zuckerman, 1995).

text.text: Theoretical accounts of psychopathy imply differential affective reactivity in both directions, such as dampened anxious or guilt-related responses to interpersonal stress among individuals high in boldness or antagonism (Blair, 2005), and heightened anger among individuals high in antagonism or disinhibition (e.g., Kosson et al., 2020).

text.text: Yet there was scant evidence that psychopathic traits moderated affective reactivity to negative interpersonal events.
Instead, there was some evidence that psychopathic traits were tied to exposure to such events.
Disinhibition was associated with more frequent stressful and unpleasant interpersonal events, but the psychopathy specifier with fewer events.

In contrast, there was evidence of cross-level moderation involving positive interpersonal events, such that higher antagonism and disinhibition (and also the total AMPD psychopathy score) were related to significantly greater positive affect following positive interpersonal interactions.
Although researchers have taken a similar approach in thinking about reactions to positive events, they have instead framed these reactions as responsivity to positive events (Zautra et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Although researchers have taken a similar approach in thinking about reactions to positive events, they have instead framed these reactions as responsivity to positive events <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Zautra et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: In our results, antagonism and disinhibition were associated with greater responsiveness to positive interpersonal events.

At the same time, disinhibition was associated with lower average positive affect across the EMA protocol, and antagonism showed a negative association of similar magnitude, although its credible interval included zero.
This suggests that individuals higher in these traits may benefit more from positive interactions when they occur, despite experiencing lower positive affect on average.
This pattern parallels findings for extraversion, where less extraverted individuals showed steeper increases in daily enjoyment following positive events (Zautra et al., 2005).
text.formatted: This pattern parallels findings for extraversion, where less extraverted individuals showed steeper increases in daily enjoyment following positive events <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Zautra et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: The finding is also somewhat surprising, because these domains, particularly antagonism, are defined in part by interpersonal styles that undermine the conditions in which positive interactions can occur (Wright et al., 2012).

text.text: However, there was no evidence that any of the AMPD psychopathy domains were related to fewer positive interpersonal interactions, on average (see Supplementary Table S4).
text.formatted: However, there was no evidence that any of the AMPD psychopathy domains were related to fewer positive interpersonal interactions, on average (see Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: Thus, whether this heightened responsiveness reflects genuine sensitivity to social reward or greater room for improvement from a lower baseline for positive affect is an important question for future work.
Overall, the present results suggest that psychopathy is not characterized by a general pattern of blunted or heightened affective reactivity to interpersonal stress in daily life.
In turn, higher averages of negative affect associated with antagonism and disinhibition could not be explained by heightened reactivity to the interpersonal events assessed here.
Nonetheless, these results cannot rule out more circumscribed deficits that arise in social contexts, or reactivity to events that may have not been assessed during the EMA protocol.

For example, the assessment approach used here could not identify interpersonal events where participants harmed another individual and thus had an opportunity to express guilt for their own behavior.

Similarly, the more notable emotional deficits linked to psychopathy involve responses to others' distress (Blair, 2005), whereas the stressors assessed here were largely self-referent (e.g., conflicts, criticism, being let down).

text.text: Importantly, the momentary findings concern affective responses to interpersonal events, even though psychopathic traits are theoretically tied to both affective and behavioral responses to interpersonal situations.

Although some daily-level results also reflect affective responses to stress (e.g., IDEP-Anger), others capture behavioral expressions of psychopathy (e.g., IDEP-Hostile Aggression) and provide distinct insights into daily-level dynamics.

The expression of psychopathy-related traits was consistently tied to days with more stressful or unpleasant interpersonal events than usual, with the exceptions of Manipulativeness, Norm Violation, and Risk-taking.
Similar to results from the momentary data, evidence of cross-level moderation was limited at the daily level.

Thus, at both the momentary and daily level, the magnitude of increases in negative affect and daily expressions of psychopathology in the context of interpersonal stress was not reliably associated with antagonism or disinhibition.

Instead, antagonism and disinhibition were associated with higher average levels of daily expressions of psychopathology relevant to psychopathy, providing further validity for the AMPD conceptualization of psychopathy as it pertains to antagonism and disinhibition.
The exceptions for cross-level moderation effects in the daily data were found for the psychopathy specifier.

Specifically, the psychopathy specifier amplified the within-person association between daily interpersonal stressors and Grandiosity/Entitlement, an effect that was consistent whether daily stress was indexed by the number of stressors or by daily mean stress ratings.
6 This moderation effect was modest in magnitude but offers some evidence that the generally adaptive profile of the psychopathy specifier may be context dependent.
Individuals high in boldness-related traits may respond to interpersonal stress with greater selfaggrandizement, at least when assessing these events at the daily level.
However, outside this exception, the psychopathy specifier demonstrated strong relations with adaptive outcomes (i.e., positive affect) and consistent negative relations with maladaptive outcomes.

Most notably, higher scores on the psychopathy specifier were related to significantly lower person-means for most IDEP facets and did not demonstrate positive associations with specific IDEP facets thought to be relevant to the construct (e.g., Risk-taking).

These divergent pattern of associations with outcomes derived from daily life raise important questions for the AMPD model of psychopathy, given that the psychopathy specifier is currently designated as an add-on element to the AMPD antisocial personality disorder diagnosis.
In the secondary models focused on mean stress ratings, the psychopathy specifier also amplified the withinperson association between daily stress and Risk-taking.
On the other hand, disinhibition dampened the same withinperson effect.

Because these effects did not emerge in the primary models using stressor counts (Supplementary Table S5), and daily stress was not associated with Risk-taking on average, they should be interpreted with these caveats in mind.

text.text: Across momentary and daily analyses, the three components of the AMPD psychopathy model showed distinct patterns of associations.

These results, focused on outcomes derived from repeated momentary and daily assessments, are consistent with findings from other study designs and assessment methods (Miller & Lynam, 2012; Blasco-Belled et al., 2024 , Sleep et al., 2019).

text.text: In turn, these findings have important consequences for how researchers and clinicians can effectively use a total AMPD score.

Because boldness-related traits are represented by the psychopathy specifier, the AMPD total score primarily reflects antagonism and disinhibition, as these two domains contribute most of its content.

Specifically, antagonism and disinhibition contribute seven facets compared to the three facets for the psychopathy specifier, although in the present study six facets from the CAT-PD were used to represent antagonism and disinhibition.
In the AMPD model of psychopathy, the psychopathy specifier is applied only in the presence of antisocial personality disorder.
Others have noted that this creates a conceptual problem (Miller et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Others have noted that this creates a conceptual problem <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Miller et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Because the specifier traits have thus far been shown to relate to adaptive functioning, including in the present study focused on outcomes from daily life, the specifier functions less as a marker of psychopathy and more as a marker of better psychological adjustment among individuals with antisocial personality disorder.

This runs counter to the dominant view developed over the past decades that psychopathy is a more severe and impairing condition than antisocial personality disorder alone (De Brito et al., 2021; Hare, 1996).

text.text: Moreover, as others have noted, it is unusual for diagnostic criteria to include features that would reduce or offset impairment (Miller et al., 2018).

text.text: The present results support these concerns surrounding the psychopathy specifier in the AMPD.

One way to reconcile these issues is to propose that the psychopathy specifier alters how antagonism and disinhibition are expressed, rather than their combination being additive in An Examination of the DSM-5 Alternative Model of Psychopathy in Daily Life nature.

Researchers have proposed curvilinear relations (e.g., Blonigen, 2013) or trait-by-trait interactions (e.g., Lilienfeld et al., 2019), in which boldness-related traits become tied to maladaptive functioning in the presence of high scores on other components of psychopathy.

Another way to reconcile the apparent adaptivity of the psychopathy specifier is that it may contribute to positive first impressions and temporarily obscure an individual's disinhibited and antagonistic interpersonal style.

Work on narcissism provides some support for this hypothesis, as narcissistic individuals are well-liked at first (Back et al., 2010), but become less popular over repeated interactions as their antagonistic behaviors become more apparent (Leckelt et al., 2015).

text.text: Examining whether the psychopathy specifier relates to favorable initial impressions that diminish over repeated interactions, and whether these effects depend on levels of antagonism or disinhibition, would be a valuable next step for future EMA and laboratory research.

However, a capacity to make favorable first impressions still reflects better interpersonal functioning, at least in the short term, which remains at odds with the view of psychopathy as a more severe condition than antisocial personality disorder alone (Miller et al., 2018).

text.text: Reconciling these issues would require evidence that this initial advantage translates into greater harm to others, for example by enabling more effective exploitation of new targets before An Examination of the DSM-5 Alternative Model of Psychopathy in Daily Life antagonistic behavior becomes apparent, and that this outcome is not achieved for individuals with elevations on antisocial personality disorder traits alone.
The present study provided the first exploration of the AMPD model of psychopathy and its relations to interpersonal stress and its consequences in daily life.
Although the results meaningfully extend past EMA work focused on psychopathy, there are important limitations of the present study that can be addressed in future research.

First, although we focused specifically on interpersonal stressful or unpleasant events, our assessment approach still combined different kinds of interpersonal events (argument/conflict vs. a promise not being kept) into a single broad category.
This may have obscured situations in which psychopathic traits did lead to greater reactivity in certain situations (e.g., provocation, reacting to others' distress).

Relatedly, because daily stressors and IDEP facets covered the same period, the daily-level models cannot disentangle whether interpersonal stressors preceded or followed the expression of psychopathic traits.
Event-contingent designs targeting specific interpersonal contexts, and momentary assessments of trait expression, would be an important improvement on the current design.

Another important limitation that has been noted in other research on the AMPD framework for psychopathy is that it is somewhat constrained in its assessment of the traits tied to psychopathy, as it does not include traits like grandiosity and (low) submissiveness, for example.
Past work has shown that the AMPD model of psychopathy can be improved, including the psychopathy specifier, by expanding its coverage of psychopathy related traits.
Thus, future EMA work can examine the utility of the current AMPD model of psychopathy compared to other approaches that expand the current AMPD model.
Last, we combined facet scales to create broader domain scores, consistent with how the AMPD operationalizes psychopathy (e.g., Wygant et al., 2020).

text.text: Our daily results also point to heterogeneity across facets in the expression of psychopathy in response to stress.
Specifically, increases in daily stress was related to greater expression of some IDEP facets but not others.

These facet-level patterns are obscured when examining domain level relations, which has been the approach in prior work examining daily stress and the IDEP in the present sample (Ringwald et al., 2025).
